title: Kaf HaChayim on Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim
heTitle: כף החיים על שולחן ערוך אורח חיים
text: (ע״ה) The Kenesset HaGedolah wrote in the rules of the decisors, letter א, in these terms: “Anything that is not mentioned in either the Babylonian Talmud or the Jerusalem Talmud, and which was not spoken of by the decisors from whom we receive the law and upon whom we rely for everything—even if the Kabbalists have spoken about it—we cannot compel those who do not follow the teachings of Kabbalah to observe it.” Thus wrote the Re’em, vol. 1, as well as the Radbaz in his responsa, vol. 1, §§ 8, 36, 49, 80, saying: “Wherever Kabbalistic teaching contradicts the Talmud, we follow the Talmud and the decisors. And if it is not mentioned in the Talmud nor among the decisors, we follow the Kabbalah.” This is also written in the Sefer Yuhasin. Likewise, Rabbi Yihya Halevi writes in a responsa, §41, in the name of Rav Shmuel Halevi: “Wherever the Zohar does not contradict the Talmud, we follow the Zohar.” And they do not disagree with the Re’em, for those authors are speaking of personal conduct that a man chooses for himself, whereas the Re’em is speaking of a case where someone does not wish to conform to the words of the Kabbalah: he cannot be compelled. End of citation. The same is found in the Magen Avraham, §20, in the Shalmei Tzibbur, p. 7c, and in others among the Aharonim. However, our master (Maran) wrote in the Beit Yosef, §141, regarding one who goes up to the Torah and whether he must read himself: “Since this is not explicitly mentioned in the Talmud, we do not reject the words of the Zohar in favor of the decisors.” See there. He wrote the same at the end of §31, see there also. Similarly, the Rav of Masseat Binyamin, §62, p. 57a, wrote: “The second path is to follow the majority in number and authority. Now the book of the Zohar carries more weight than all the authors who came after the close of the Talmud, and if all those authors were placed on one side of the scale and the Zohar alone on the other, it would outweigh them all. Therefore it is preferable to the majority of decisors, as the Beit Yosef wrote, that we follow the Zohar against other authors.” End of citation. The same is written by the pious Rabbi Avraham Riqueti in Aderet Eliyahu, pamphlet Tefillin de Maarei Alma, p. 15b, and also by the Rav of Beit Dineno Shel Shlomo, §12, concerning this rule. He cited the words of Maran in the Beit Yosef, as well as those of the Masseat Binyamin, and he expressed astonishment that Rav Mahari Habib, in his rules, did not mention these words of Maran, which appear to contradict those of the Re’em and the Radbaz. He wrote that even according to Rav Shmuel Halevi and the Sefer Yuhasin, their view aligns with that of the Beit Yosef, and how then could it be said that they do not disagree? See there. However, the Rav in the Darkei Moshe, §141, letter ב, contradicts Maran and writes: “One must not depart from the decisors, even if the words of the Zohar disagree with them, and not like the Beit Yosef, etc.” End of citation. This also emerges from the Derisha, see there. See also Pitchei Teshuva, letter ה, which brings all the opinions mentioned, see there. See also Divrei Menachem, letter ט, in the name of the Haim Tov, who writes that in case of controversy among the decisors, it is the words of Kabbalah that decide, see there. It follows that the Radbaz, the Re’em, and the Rama hold that one must follow the decisors against the Zohar, while Maran, Rav Shmuel Halevi, the Sefer Yuhasin, and the Masseat Binyamin hold that one follows the words of the Zohar and the Kabbalists against the decisors, in anything that was not explicitly decided in the Talmud. And it follows that even in matters of doubt concerning blessings (safek berakhot), if not explicitly mentioned in the Talmud, we follow the Kabbalists against the decisors, and we do not say “safek berakhot lehaqel.” This is also written by the Birkei Yosef, §46, letter י״א, concerning the blessing “hanoten la-yaef koach,” which is not mentioned in the Talmud, as explained in the Beit Yosef. And the Birkei Yosef wrote: “Today, the custom has spread in our lands to recite this blessing according to the writings of the Ari zal, for even though we have accepted the rulings of Maran, it is certain that if Maran had seen the view of the holy Ari, he too would have admitted that it must be recited.” End of citation. Here then are the explicit words of the Birkei Yosef according to the view of Maran: although he wrote in the Beit Yosef that according to the Rambam, the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, and the Rokeah one should not recite this blessing, if he had seen the words of the Arizal, he would have recited it, without regard for the principle of safek berakhot lehaqel when set against the Arizal. This is also what the Ben Ish Chai wrote, Parashat Bereshit letter י, and Parashat Vayeshev letter ה, that in the face of the opinion of our master the Ari zal, we do not say safek berakhot lehaqel. And indeed, the custom of the world is not to be concerned with safek berakhot when set against the words of the Arizal, for regarding the morning blessings—even if one is not personally obligated to recite them—there is controversy about reciting them, as clarified in §46, paragraph 8, yet the custom of the world is to recite them according to the words of the Arizal in the Shaar HaKavanot, p. 1c, where it is written that one is obligated to recite them each day even if not personally obligated. See there. And this will be further clarified in §46, with God’s help!

18) Ibid: Who are accustomed to going out, etc. [Regarding] those women who come from lands in which their custom is not to show [ their hair] to a place in which their custom is to show it, they are permitted to show it if they are not planning to go back. Maharam AlShaker 35; Magen Avraham, minor note 4; SuB 2. However, in the Zohar, Parashat Nasso 125b, it was very strict about a woman's hair, such that none of it should be seen outside, and this is its wording there: Rabbi Chizkiah said, "Cursed be the man who allows his wife to let the hair of her head be seen. This is one of the rules of modesty in the house. A woman who exposes her hair for self-adornment brings poverty on her household, renders her children of no account in their generation, and causes another thing to abide in her house. If this is so in the house, how much more is it when in the marketplace; and ever so much more so does all this result from another kind of shamelessness. And because of this, it is written, Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine within your house (Psalms 128:3)." Rabbi Yehudah said, "Hair of the head of a woman being exposed leads to hair of another kind being exposed and impaired. Hence a woman should not let her hair be seen, even by the beams of her house, much less outside. Come and see that as the rule is most strict in the case of a man’s hair, so is it with a woman’s. Consider how much harm a woman’s hair brings about, what it causes above, and what it causes below. It brings a curse on her husband, it causes poverty, it causes something else to happen to her household, it causes the inferiority of her children. May the Merciful One deliver us from their impudence! A woman thus should cover her hair in the four comers of her house. When she does this, what is written? Your children will be like olive trees. As the olive does not shed its leaves either in autumn or summer, but ever retains its superiority over other trees, so her children will excel over other people of the world; her husband, moreover, will receive blessings from above and from below, will be blessed with riches, with children and children’s children. So this is [the meaning of] that which is written, Behold, surely, thus shall the man be blessed…. [And see your children’s children, peace be upon Israel] (Psalms 128:4[-6])." To here are its [words]. And SuB cites its words there.

271) There — since they do not raise their palms (to say the priestly blessing) except on holidays, etc. The Agur wrote that he was asked by RI Mulin why the priests do not raise their palms every day, given that it is a positive commandment. And he answered [that] it is because the custom of the priests is first to immerse [in a ritual bath], as it is written in the Hagahot Maimoniot, such that it is difficult for them to immerse in the winter. Hence the custom arose to do it only on holidays. And it is also by reason of [not wanting to] miss work. And when a priest is not called up, he does not transgress [the negation of this positive commandment]. To here are his [words]. And the Beit Yosef cited him and wrote about him; and these are his words: He stretched himself too far to defend the custom of his place, but it is not enough. For that which he wrote [that] it is because we follow the practice of immersing first — that is a stringency that leads to a leniency! And it makes that which is taught [in a baraita] dependent on that which is not taught [meaning, it is unduly prioritizing something the source of which is less authoritative]. For behold, immersion for raising the palms is not mentioned in the Talmud. So even if they followed the stringency of immersing, why should they, on account of that, nullify three positive commandments every day? And even if he does not transgress unless he is called, it is nevertheless preferable for them to fulfill three positive commandments every day and not negate them, given that they are not obligated to immerse and, as a result, leave off from fulfilling three positive commandments every day. And [more correct] are the residents of the land of Israel and the whole kingdom of Egypt who raise their palms every day and do not immerse [themselves first] to raise their palms. To here are his [words]. However our master Rabbi Moshe [Isserles], may his memory be blessed, wrote in the Darkhei Moseh, note 21, "The reason is because they are preoccupied with their sustenance and are not filled with joy. Hence they do not raise their palms every day, etc." — and as he wrote here in the gloss. But Rama MiPano, may his memory be blessed, wrote in paragraph 95 that that which the world follows the practice that the priests do not go up on the platform [to recite the priestly blessing] on any of the days of the year, whether weekday or Shabbat, besides on holidays is a defective custom, see there. And the Knesset HaGedolah [R. Chaim Benvenisti] cited him in the gloss on the Beit Yosef at the end of the paragraph and in the Shayarei Knesset HaGedolah in the gloss on the Beit Yosef, note 27, Magen Avraham, small note 70. And in the Shayarei Knesset HaGedolah there, he wrote that they do not follow the practice that our master Rabbi Moshe, may his memory be blessed, wrote. And so wrote the Olat Tamid [R. Chaim Vital], note 100: As it is fitting and correct in every place not to follow the practice not to find machinations to negate a positive commandment in the Torah; even though the priest does not transgress unless they call him. For regardless, bounty and blessing come to the world through the priestly blessing. To here are his words. And likewise did he write above, note 262, in the name of the Sha'ar HaKavanot that raising the palms is one of the [items] required for the rectification of prayer and it needs to take place every day during the repetition of the prayer leader. And see further in our words above, note 16.

Sur les légumes, on bénit "Boré Péri Haadama". Et si on s’est trompé et qu’on a béni sur les légumes "Boré Miné Deshaïm" (Créateur des différentes herbes), on est quitte a posteriori. Le Rav Richon LeTsion dans sa méthode, Yoreh Deah fin du chapitre 71. Et selon cela, il en va de même si on a béni sur les légumineuses "Boré Miné Zéraïm" (Créateur des différentes graines), on est quitte a posteriori. Mais il y a un doute si on a béni sur les légumes "Boré Miné Zéraïm" (au lieu de "Boré Péri Haadama"), si l’on est quitte. Voir Birkei Yosef, paragraphe 4, mais le Shaarei Teshuva, paragraphe 1, pense que c’est évident qu’on est quitte, car il est écrit : "Et comme un jardin fait pousser ses semences", voir là-bas.

"Mais la courge, la betterave et le chou, etc." Et s’ils sont marinés, ils sont considérés comme consommables crus et on bénira "Boré Péri Haadama". Voir Shlah, qui a été cité par le Maguen Avraham, paragraphe 2. Et ainsi a écrit le Taz, paragraphe 1. Et ainsi est écrit dans le Shoulkhan Aroukh plus loin dans ce chapitre concernant le navet. Et le Maguen Avraham a écrit là-bas que d’après la Guemara, un aliment salé est comme cuit pour cette question. Et on voit aussi qu’il est meilleur lorsqu’il est salé.

Oil with fragrance, like the anointing oil, etc. The one who makes the anointing oil according to the prescribed method and measurement as stated in the Torah is liable for karet (excision) if done intentionally, and liable for a sin offering (ḥatat) if done unintentionally. This applies only if it is made for anointing purposes. However, if it was made for study purposes or to give to others, one is exempt. This is discussed in the Rambam, Chapter 1 of the Laws of the Holy Temple. Similarly, the one who makes incense according to the eleven signs mentioned and uses the proper measurements is also liable for karet, even if only half or a third of the amount was made, as long as it was done according to the prescribed measurements. If done for study purposes or for public use, one is exempt. This is discussed in the Rambam, Chapter 2, Laws of Incense.
One recites “Who creates various kinds of fragrances” (borei minei besamim) This is because “various kinds of fragrances” encompasses all types of fragrances. This is explained in the Tur and Levush.
It is a fragrance without substance This means that the fragrance does not come from the substance of the oil itself. This is discussed in the Tur.

It is a fragrance without substance This is not the same as the rose water discussed in Section 3, where one recites “Who creates fragrant trees” (borei atzei besamim). In that case, it is referring to the situation where the roses were squeezed for their water or cooked in water until the essence of the fruit dissolved into the water, as mentioned earlier in Section 41, where the fragrance does have substance. In contrast, here, there is only the fragrance without the substance.

It is a fragrance without substance Therefore, tobacco and other substances inhaled through the nose should not have a blessing recited over them if they contain a pleasant fragrance, since they are considered fragrances without substance. This is explained earlier in Siman 210, Section 33.

It is a fragrance without substance This is why it is customary for the meticulous to avoid reciting the blessing over the fragrance of wooden vessels that have been used to grind spices, as it is also considered a fragrance without substance. This is discussed in Rav Shlomo Luria, Attaẓ in Section 2, and Beit Yosef in Siman 217, Section 2, where it is stated that no blessing should be recited over it.

Since it is a matter of doubt, it is proper to be cautious and avoid smelling it This applies when one only has this specific oil and no other fragrances are available. However, if other fragrances are available, one may recite a blessing over them, with the intention of including this particular fragrance as well. This is explained in the Tur, Levush, and other authorities. If one absorbed the fragrance of fragrant trees, he is exempt with the blessing of “Who creates fragrant trees”; similarly, if he absorbed the fragrance of herbs, he is exempt with the blessing of “Who creates fragrant herbs”. If both types of fragrance were absorbed, he is exempt with the blessing of “Who creates various kinds of fragrances”. This applies even if the fragrance he absorbed was only from trees or herbs, as “various kinds” covers all fragrances.

It is proper to be cautious and avoid smelling it One should also be cautious about smelling pepper and ginger because some authorities hold that no blessing should be recited over them, as explained in Ateret Zekeinim, Siman 297, Section 1. This is also confirmed in Chida’s Chaim Avraham, Section 61, and Kitzur Shulchan Aruch, Siman 58, Section 3.

Who are merciful towards them for if they are not merciful towards them, we are concerned in case in the person's heart they interpret the dream not for the good. And even though "words in the heart are not words" (this mental action should not be effective), in any case there is what to be concerned about -- perhaps we are worried in case they go after others and say "Ploni saw a dream which is not good".

27And one reads the haftara of the Chariot of Ezekiel, etc.: And the reason is that it is written in the Zohar Chadash that Ezekiel saw the chariot on the day of Shavuot — Mahari Lingo in a manuscript. But the words of the Zohar are not understandable, since it is written: in the fourth [month], etc. (Ezekiel 1:1) — Birkei Yosef 3. However, in [the same author, Chaim Yosef David Azulay's] book, Machzik Berakhah, he wrote to resolve this according to what he found in Hagahot HaRamaz on the words of the Zohar mentioned [above], see there. However, it can also be said that the reason that we read the haftara of the Chariot of Ezekiel is because there are visions of the divine presence written in it, and the Jewish people saw visions of the divine presence at the stand at Mount Sinai on that day [Shavuot]. And, if so, it is from the topic of the day.

41) Ibid., And each one must send two portions to his fellow, etc.: In the Binyan Tzion responsa, section 44, he questions whether if one brought the portion himself, and not through a messenger, if he has fulfilled [the commandment]. Since it is written, "and sending," we can say that we need it to be specifically through a messenger, see there. But it appears to me that one cannot be exacting about it only being through a messenger. For behold, we have found the expression, "sending," in several places, and it is not with a messenger. As it is written with Noach (Genesis 8:9), "and he sent out his hand and took it." And with Avraham (Genesis 22:10), "And Avraham sent out his hand." And (Deuteronomy 15:13), "When you send him free from you." And there are many like these. Nevertheless, if it is possible, it should be done with a messenger on account of the honor. But if it is impossible, the commandment should not be negated on account of this. And that is simple.
